idea.title: Drift Harp
idea.pitch: A harp of plucked strings that you strum by dragging a finger or cursor across them, each string a Karplus-Strong plucked string tuned in pure just intonation and shown on a live fifths-and-thirds lattice. Play a looping chord progression and hear and see the pitch creep up by a syntonic comma (about a fifth of a semitone) every lap, a trick called a comma pump. A tempering dial lets you squeeze the drift shut and hear exactly what equal temperament trades away.
idea.whyNow: Timeless: a tuning-system explorer where the surprise is audible. The visitor discovers on their own that pure intervals do not close a loop, which most explainers only state in words.

research.summary: A comma pump is a repeating progression whose pure intervals almost, but not exactly, return to the start, so the pitch shifts by a small interval each lap. The standard case is the syntonic comma (81:80, about 21.5 cents) in the progression C G D A E C; both Wikipedia and the Xenharmonic Wiki describe it. A 5-limit just intonation lattice puts fifths (3/2) on one axis and major thirds (5/4) on the other, so a loop that does not close is the drift made visible. Karplus-Strong gives a cheap plucked string: a noise burst circulating in a delay line with an averaging filter, where loop length sets pitch and the filter sets decay. Browser Karplus-Strong demos exist (one was seen), which de-risks the sound engine, but none found combines it with a drifting lattice.

sources.title: Comma pump
sources.snippet: Describes a comma pump as a sequence, often chords, that shifts pitch by a small interval each repetition; the usual example is C G D A E C raising pitch by 81:80 in just intonation.
sources.note: Found again by search on 2026-10-12 (Comma pump article: sequence, often chords, shifting pitch by a comma each pass; C G D A E C raises it by 81:80).

sources.title: Comma pump (Xenharmonic Wiki)
sources.snippet: Independent wiki entry covering comma pumps: loops of just intervals that nearly close, tempered out in systems that equate the comma to unison.
sources.note: Found again by search; xenharmonic wiki entry on comma pumps, independent of Wikipedia.

sources.title: Just Intonation: pitch drift explanation (FIU)
sources.snippet: University page explaining that in just intonation one note name can have several pitches a syntonic comma (about 21.5 cents) apart, and that choirs meet this as drift.
sources.note: Not found again in the 2026-10-12 results; the 21.5 cent size is carried by the xen.wiki 81/80 entry and Wikipedia comma articles instead.

sources.title: Karplus-Strong string synthesis
sources.snippet: Physical-modelling method: a burst of noise recirculates through a filtered delay line; loop length sets pitch, filter sets decay. Invented by Alexander Strong and analysed by Kevin Karplus.
sources.note: Found again by search at the Wikipedia address (the page itself could not be fetched). Algorithm definition and history.

sources.title: Karplus Strong Algorithm (CCRMA, Stanford)
sources.snippet: Stanford physical audio signal processing text on the Karplus-Strong algorithm, a delay line with a lowpass in the feedback loop.
sources.note: Not found again at this address; the Blynn Stanford page, Csound manual and others carry the same method.

sources.title: Lattice (music)
sources.snippet: Pitch lattices place just ratios on axes by prime; the 5-limit lattice uses 3/2 and 5/4, drawn as square or hexagonal grids; the gap between a 5/4 third and the Pythagorean third is the syntonic comma.
sources.note: Found again by search on 2026-10-12 together with xen.wiki 5-limit and a music-theory article: vertical axis fifths 3/2, horizontal axis thirds 5/4.

sources.title: karplus stress tester (GitHub)
sources.snippet: A browser project that plucks virtual Karplus-Strong strings as a custom audio processing exercise; notes glitches when the browser cannot keep up.
sources.note: Not found again by search; kept only as a performance warning that voice counts must be budgeted.

sources.title: Interval information: 81/80
sources.snippet: Xenharmonic wiki entry on the ratio 81/80, the syntonic comma, about 21.5 cents.
sources.note: Independent confirmation of the comma size and name.

sources.title: Comma (music)
sources.snippet: Wikipedia article on commas, including the syntonic comma as the gap between a Pythagorean ditone (81:64) and a just major third (5:4).
sources.note: Second site confirming the 81:80 ratio and the roughly 21.5 cent size.

sources.title: The Karplus-Strong Algorithm
sources.snippet: Explainer: a buffer of random values is repeatedly averaged, the loop length sets the pitch and averaging damps high harmonics faster.
sources.note: Independent of Wikipedia; also notes the half-sample delay and the tuning error from integer loop lengths.

sources.title: Csound manual: pluck opcode
sources.snippet: Manual page for a plucked-string opcode with simple and stretched averaging decay methods.
sources.note: Third independent description of the Karplus-Strong decay methods.

sources.title: 5 limit (Xenharmonic Wiki)
sources.snippet: Wiki entry on the 5-limit: a two-dimensional lattice of pitch classes built from fifths and major thirds.
sources.note: Second source for the lattice axes.

facts.claim: A comma pump is a progression that returns almost, but not exactly, to its starting pitch, shifting by a small interval each repetition; the classic syntonic example is C G D A E C, rising by 81:80 per lap in just intonation, and the pump closes exactly in 12-tone equal temperament (Wikipedia and Xenharmonic Wiki, as of 2026-10-12).
The syntonic comma is the ratio 81:80, about 21.5 cents, the gap between a Pythagorean ditone (81:64) and a just major third (5:4) (Xenharmonic Wiki and Wikipedia, as of 2026-10-12).

Karplus-Strong synthesis circulates a burst of noise through a delay line with an averaging low-pass filter; loop length sets pitch and the filter shapes decay, so high harmonics fade faster (Wikipedia, a Stanford explainer and the Csound manual, as of 2026-10-12).
A 5-limit pitch lattice puts just fifths (3/2) on one axis and just major thirds (5/4) on the other (Wikipedia Lattice article and Xenharmonic Wiki 5-limit entry, as of 2026-10-12).

inspirations: pitch lattice diagrams from xenharmonic tuning software

design.coreLoop: Drag across strings to strum, assemble a short loop of chords on the lattice, and let it cycle. Each lap the drift meter shows the pure tuning rising by one syntonic comma while a ghost of the starting pitch stays put. Turn the tempering dial to close the loop and hear what is lost, or chase a lap that lands back home using adaptive retuning. Every chord choice changes how fast and which way the pitch wanders, so there is always another loop to try.
sophisticationHooks: Karplus-Strong voices with per-string damping, pick position and a stroke-speed-dependent excitation, polyphonic across a harp of 12 strings
Live 5-limit pitch lattice with ratio and cents readouts; the drift is the distance between where a loop starts and where it ends on the lattice
Tempering dial that continuously morphs pure ratios toward 12-tone equal temperament, with a seeded generative drone that makes beating audible
Shareable URL hash holding the chord loop, tempering amount and seed
design.scopeForOneDay: Shrunk and de-risked. Build: Karplus-Strong plucks rendered on demand into AudioBuffers in the main thread (no AudioWorklet, so no CSP issue) with a voice pool, 12 strings, canvas harp and lattice views, pointer/touch strum and keyboard play, loop editor with 6 slots, drift meter with a ghost of the starting pitch, tempering dial, a muted-state visual story (lattice path, cents readout), URL-hash share, about panel. Cut: AudioWorklet, MIDI export, 7-limit and higher primes, recording, presets beyond three.
risks: AudioWorklet from a blob or inline module may be blocked by the page CSP; the plan renders each pluck into an AudioBuffer instead, which needs no worklet.
Audio only starts after a user gesture and a headless screenshot cannot hear it, so the lattice path, drift meter and cents readout must carry the story when muted.

Voice cost: each pluck buffer is generated in JavaScript; short buffers (about 2 seconds) and a voice cap keep it responsive, as the stress-test project warns of glitches when the browser cannot keep up (that project was not found again, so it is not cited as fact).

The pump claim is solid, but the audible effect depends on voice-leading that keeps every chord pure; the spec fixes four tested loops, including the C G D A E C case, and checks the lap drift numerically in a unit test.
Unverified sources: the FIU drift page, the CCRMA Stanford page and the karplus stress tester were not found again; the page cites only sources seen on 2026-10-12.

verification.notes: Comma pump, 81:80 at about 21.5 cents, Karplus-Strong and the 5-limit lattice axes were each found in independent results (WebFetch to ccrma.stanford.edu, en.xen.wiki and justintonation.fiu.edu failed at DNS). Buildable in a morning if plucks render to AudioBuffers; no data needed.
